definition: A manufactured fiber or filament finer than a conventional threshold, often set at 1 decitex (0.1 tex) per filament, used for soft, dense fabrics and cleaning cloths.
explanation: Microfiber is a size category, not a polymer. Polyester, nylon and other polymers can be made as microfibers by spinning very fine filaments directly, or by spinning bicomponent filaments that are later split apart or have one component dissolved away. Finer filaments bend more easily, so a yarn with many fine filaments is softer and drapes better than one with fewer coarse filaments of the same total linear density. The much larger surface area per gram gives microfiber fabrics strong wicking and particle capture, and their dense packing makes them wind resistant while still passing water vapor.
example: A class compares two polyester yarns of the same total linear density, one made of 36 filaments and one of 144. The 144-filament yarn has much finer filaments, so it feels softer and packs into a denser woven cloth. Calculating surface area per gram for both shows why the finer yarn picks up more oil when wiped across a greasy surface.
caution: Microfiber describes filament fineness, not fiber type, recycled content or environmental performance. In environmental science the same word is used for fiber pieces shed during washing, a separate topic covered under fiber fragment release. Thresholds are not harmonized across sources and units; a limit written as 1 denier is about 11% coarser than 1 dtex. Ask for the polymer and the linear density per filament.
deeper: A review of melt-spun fibers gives standard multifilaments as about 10 to 40 micrometers per filament, which for PET corresponds to roughly 0.1 to 1.7 tex, and defines a microfiber as below 0.1 tex. The unit arithmetic: 1 denier is 1 gram per 9,000 m and 1 decitex is 1 gram per 10,000 m, so 1 denier equals about 1.11 dtex. For a round filament, diameter in micrometers is about 11.28 x sqrt(dtex / density in g/cm3); a 1 dtex PET filament (density about 1.38) is roughly 9.6 micrometers across. Ultrafine fibers below 1 micrometer come from bicomponent routes: segmented-pie filaments of two poorly adhering polymers split under mechanical stress, while islands-in-the-sea filaments have their matrix dissolved to release the embedded fibrils.
origins: The word joins micro with fiber and first named deliberately engineered ultrafine synthetic filaments. Producing them at scale depended on bicomponent melt spinning, which the review cited here dates to the 1960s, and on splitting or dissolving steps that free fine filaments from a composite fiber. Later, environmental researchers adopted microfiber for fibers shed from clothing in washing-machine effluent, which is why the word now carries two quite different meanings.

definition: The mass of water a fiber holds, expressed as a percentage of its oven-dry mass, once it has come to equilibrium with a stated atmosphere of temperature and relative humidity.
explanation: Fibers exchange water vapor with the surrounding air until they reach equilibrium. Moisture regain expresses the water held relative to dry fiber mass, so it can be compared across fibers and used to correct traded weights. Hydrophilic fibers with many accessible polar groups, such as wool and cellulose, hold much more water than hydrophobic synthetics. Because equilibrium depends on temperature, humidity and on whether the fiber is gaining or losing water, regain must always be quoted with its conditioning atmosphere.
example: A wool buyer receives two bales of equal invoice weight, one shipped from a humid port and one from a dry inland store. Laboratory oven-drying shows the first contains noticeably more water. Correcting both to the agreed commercial regain shows the buyer paid for the same amount of fiber only once the water is accounted for.
caution: Moisture regain is not the same as moisture content, which divides water by total wet mass, and it is not a measure of liquid absorbency or wicking. Values also show hysteresis: a fiber approaching equilibrium from the wet side holds more water than one approaching from the dry side. Commercial or conventional regains are agreed trading values, not measurements of a particular lot.
deeper: Regain R = 100 x (conditioned mass minus oven-dry mass) / oven-dry mass, while moisture content M = 100 x water / conditioned mass, so M = 100R / (100 + R); a regain of 15% equals a moisture content of about 13%. Values are normally quoted for a standard atmosphere, commonly 20 C and 65% relative humidity. Typical figures under such conditions are roughly 14 to 18% for wool, about 11% for silk and lyocell, a few percent for nylon, and well under 1% for polyester, where laboratory measurements on fabrics have reported about 0.2 to 0.4%. Sorption depends on accessible polar groups (hydroxyls in cellulose, amide and ionic side groups in keratin), which lie mainly in less ordered regions, so higher crystallinity lowers regain. Fiber-characterization studies commonly cite ASTM D2654 for regain and moisture content.
origins: The word describes the water that oven-dried fiber regains from the air. Because wool, silk and cotton are sold by weight and absorb water, traders needed agreed allowances so that buyers did not pay fiber prices for water, and fixed commercial regains grew out of that need. Wool testing still reports fiber on a conditioned basis: a 2023 study of four Ethiopian breeds, for example, reported raw wool regains of about 9 to 17% alongside clean yield measured to an IWTO standard.

definition: Momme is a traditional Japanese-derived unit used to express silk fabric weight; one momme corresponds to about 4.34 grams per square meter.
explanation: Momme began as a Japanese unit of mass, fixed at 3.75 grams in the Meiji era, and the silk trade adopted it as a fabric weight grade. In English-language trade it is commonly defined as the weight in pounds of a silk piece 45 inches wide and 100 yards long, which works out to about 4.34 g/m2 per momme. Higher momme means more silk per unit area, which often goes with greater opacity and body.
example: A buyer compares a 19 momme charmeuse with a 22 momme charmeuse. Multiplying by about 4.34 gives roughly 82 g/m2 and 95 g/m2. The difference is about 15 percent more silk per square meter in the heavier fabric. That is a meaningful mass difference, but the buyer still needs to compare weave, yarn and finishing before predicting drape or durability.
caution: Momme is a weight measure only; it does not state weave, thread count, fiber grade or whether sericin has been removed. It is mainly meaningful for silk, where trade practice defines it, and applying it to other fibers invites confusion. Small differences in quoted conversion factors, such as 4.33 versus 4.34 g/m2, reflect rounding rather than different units.
deeper: The conversion can be checked arithmetically. A piece 45 inches by 100 yards measures about 1.143 m by 91.44 m, or about 104.5 m2. One pound is about 453.6 g, so 453.6 divided by 104.5 gives roughly 4.34 g/m2 for each momme, or about 3.62 grams per square yard. The original mass unit, 3.75 g, is a separate quantity: momme as a mass unit and momme as a silk weight grade share a name but not dimensions. Because silk is often degummed after weaving, and degumming removes sericin mass, the stage at which a fabric is weighed affects the figure. Laboratory confirmation uses an ordinary mass-per-area method on conditioned specimens.
origins: The monme belonged to the traditional Japanese system of weights and served as both a unit of mass and a monetary weight. During the Meiji era it was fixed at exactly 3.75 grams. Its use as a silk grade carried over into international trade, where the fabric-grade definition used in English-language commerce recasts it in inches, yards and pounds. Trade literature is inconsistent about the precise history, so treat detailed origin stories with caution.
